title: Unilateral tinnitus with asymmetric hearing loss

patient.name: Anjali
patient.intro: Anjali has come to the clinic because of a persistent sound in her left ear. She appears worried and is waiting for you to begin the consultation.

turns.patient: I've been hearing this ringing in my left ear. It's been worrying me.
turns.prompt: How will you begin the consultation?

options.text: Tell me more about the sound and what you have noticed about it.
Don't worry. Tinnitus is usually harmless.
Let's skip the history and start the hearing test.

turns.patient: It is mostly there every day. I first noticed it about six months ago.

patientByTrust.low: I suppose it has been there for months. I don't know how much I should tell you.
patientByTrust.high: Yes, it is there most days. I noticed it about six months ago, and I feel comfortable telling you more about it.

turns.prompt: Which question is most useful next?

options.text: Is the sound in one ear or both, and is it rhythmic or pulse-synchronous?
Do you normally watch television at night?
Are you sure it is really tinnitus?

turns.patient: Only my left ear. It isn't beating with my pulse. I also feel like my hearing on that side isn't as good as it used to be.

patientByTrust.low: Only my left ear. I haven't really said much because I feel like I'm not being listened to.
patientByTrust.high: Only my left ear. It isn't beating with my pulse. I also feel like my hearing on that side isn't as good as it used to be.

turns.prompt: The patient has now disclosed unilateral symptoms and perceived hearing difficulty. What should you explore?

options.text: Ask about sudden changes, neurological symptoms, ear history, noise exposure and other associated symptoms.
Tell her that unilateral tinnitus is common and move directly to treatment.
Ask only how loud the tinnitus feels.

turns.patient: I'm mainly afraid that something serious could be causing it. I just want to know what is happening.

patientByTrust.low: I'm still worried, and I'm not sure I understand what is happening. I just want someone to take my concern seriously.
patientByTrust.high: I'm mainly afraid that something serious could be causing it. I appreciate you explaining what you are looking for. I just want to know what is happening.

turns.prompt: How will you respond before moving to diagnostic testing?

options.text: Acknowledge the concern, explain that you will investigate the pattern carefully, and tell her what the next steps are.
reveals: Patient wants explanation and next steps

options.text: There is no reason to be worried until we find something.
I can't say anything until after the test.

stages.title: 1. Integrate the clinical story
stages.prompt: After your patient interaction, which feature should receive particular attention?

options.text: Persistent unilateral tinnitus with asymmetric hearing findings
Only tinnitus loudness
Whether the patient likes hearing aids

stages.feedback: The interaction has revealed unilateral tinnitus, perceived hearing reduction and concern. Laterality and asymmetry are key features.

stages.title: 2. Interpret the findings
stages.prompt: The case includes asymmetric SNHL, normal tympanograms and absent left acoustic reflexes. What is the appropriate interpretation?

options.text: The pattern warrants consideration of a retrocochlear red flag and further medical evaluation
The findings confirm a benign tinnitus cause
Normal tympanograms rule out further referral

stages.feedback: The supplied findings are intended to represent a retrocochlear red-flag pattern requiring appropriate referral rather than a definitive diagnosis.

stages.title: 3. Check for red flags
stages.prompt: What should the student do with this presentation?

options.text: Recognize unilateral/asymmetric findings as a referral trigger and recommend appropriate ENT/medical assessment
Proceed directly to sound therapy without referral
Ignore asymmetry because tinnitus is common

stages.feedback: The protocol explicitly identifies unilateral non-pulsatile tinnitus with asymmetric hearing loss as a retrocochlear red flag.

stages.title: 4. Select management
stages.prompt: What is the appropriate immediate management direction?

options.text: Prioritize medical/ENT evaluation before treating the tinnitus as an uncomplicated presentation
Fit hearing aids immediately without further assessment
Recommend complete sound avoidance

stages.feedback: Referral is the priority when the specified red-flag pattern is present.

stages.title: 5. Justify the decision

options.text: Unilateral tinnitus plus asymmetric hearing findings can indicate a need to investigate retrocochlear pathology, so referral is appropriate
All unilateral tinnitus is automatically a confirmed tumor
The audiogram is irrelevant to tinnitus reasoning

stages.feedback: The case supports concern and referral, not a definitive diagnosis. The distinction is important for clinical reasoning.

stages.title: 6. Plan follow-up
stages.prompt: After referral, what should audiology contribute?

options.text: Track hearing/tinnitus status and incorporate medical findings into later individualized management
Close the case permanently
Monitor only tinnitus pitch

stages.feedback: Follow-up should integrate subsequent medical information with ongoing hearing and tinnitus needs.
